Your DesignPD scores reveal how your design tends to move through three behavioral patterns: planning, decision making, and action. These tendencies do not measure ability or potential. Instead, they highlight the natural ways your design most often prepares, processes information, and moves forward.

While DesignID helps you understand identity through the reflections of Architect, Artisan, Shepherd, and Steward, DesignPD explores how that design translates into preparation, judgment, and execution within everyday situations such as leadership, collaboration, conflict, pressure, and sustainability.

From Insight to Application

Your DesignID results help reveal who you are by showing how your life most naturally reflects the image of God through the four core reflections: Architect, Artisan, Shepherd, and Steward. These reflections shape the way you see, serve, relate, and contribute.

DesignPD builds on that foundation by exploring how your design operates in real life. Through the lenses of Plan, Decide, and Do, this report highlights how your reflection patterns move into preparation, discernment, and action.

The following pages apply your design to five areas of impact where your tendencies become especially visible. These environments move from strength and contribution into strain and long term stewardship, helping you see how your design responds across the realities of leadership and life.

On Purpose — For Purpose

which God prepared in advance for us to do.” — Ephesians 2:10
Your design is not accidental. God has uniquely shaped your reflections, capacities, and tendencies so that your life can contribute meaningfully across the environments He has prepared you to walk through.

Your tendencies in Plan, Decide, and Do influence how you frame the issue, how you interpret what is happening, and how you move toward resolution. Understanding these patterns can help you respond with greater awareness, steadiness, and wisdom.

How the Core Reflections Often Respond to Conflict

Architect
Architects often respond to conflict by identifying the core issue and pushing for clarity or resolution. Their instinct is to address the problem directly and move toward a solution.

Artisan
Artisans often respond to conflict through interpretation, nuance, and expression. Their instinct is to understand what is being communicated beneath the surface and bring clarity to what feels misunderstood.

Shepherd
Shepherds often experience conflict through its relational impact. Their instinct is to protect connection, reduce harm, and help people feel heard and restored.

Steward
Stewards often respond to conflict by seeking order, responsibility, and appropriate structure. Their instinct is to stabilize the situation and reestablish what is fair, clear, and dependable.

Your conflict response may be strengthened or strained depending on specific capacity. When capacity is steady or abundant, clarity and maturity tend to increase. When capacity is limited or drained, reactivity, fatigue, or avoidance may become more likely.

Conflict does not only reveal tension. It also reveals where growth, maturity, and wise leadership can emerge when your design is stewarded well.

Toward Peace

Conflict handled wisely is not merely about ending tension. It is about moving toward truth, peace, and restored relationship where possible. Conflict can become a place where clarity deepens, humility grows, and peace is pursued with greater intention.

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.” — Matthew 5:9

How the Core Reflections Often Approach Collaboration

Architect
Architects often approach collaboration by helping establish direction, clarify goals, and move the group toward purposeful progress. Their instinct is to bring initiative and forward momentum to shared work.

Artisan
Artisans often approach collaboration through insight, interpretation, and communication. Their instinct is to bring clarity, nuance, and thoughtful expression that helps the group better understand ideas and possibilities.

Shepherd
Shepherds often approach collaboration by fostering trust, inclusion, and relational awareness. Their instinct is to create an environment where people feel valued, heard, and able to contribute.

Steward
Stewards often approach collaboration by bringing consistency, responsibility, and dependable follow through. Their instinct is to support shared work through order, stability, and practical care for what has been entrusted.

Your collaborative patterns may be strengthened or strained depending on specific capacity. When capacity is steady or abundant, collaboration often becomes clearer, more generous, and more productive. When capacity is limited or drained, withdrawal, overextension, or misalignment may become more likely.

Collaboration does not only reveal how you work with others. It also reveals how your design contributes to shared purpose, mutual support, and stronger outcomes when stewarded well.

Toward Unity

Healthy collaboration is not merely about working beside one another. It is about moving in shared purpose with humility, clarity, and mutual care. Collaboration can become a place where unity deepens, trust grows, and collective strength is expressed more fully.

“Make every effort to keep the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace.” — Ephesians 4:3

How the Core Reflections Often Approach Leadership

Architect
Architects often approach leadership by creating direction, initiating movement, and helping others see what could be built or pursued. Their instinct is to lead with vision, courage, and forward momentum.

Artisan
Artisans often approach leadership through insight, discernment, and thoughtful expression. Their instinct is to help others see with greater clarity, understand meaning more deeply, and move with wiser perspective.

Shepherd
Shepherds often approach leadership by caring for people, building trust, and creating environments where others can grow. Their instinct is to lead with relational awareness, encouragement, and compassion.

Steward
Stewards often approach leadership by bringing consistency, responsibility, and dependable structure. Their instinct is to support people and mission through faithful oversight, clear expectations, and steady follow through.

Your leadership patterns may be strengthened or strained depending on which specific capacity. When capacity is steady or abundant, leadership often becomes clearer, more grounded, and more life giving. When capacity is limited or drained, overextension, hesitation, or imbalance may become more likely.

Leadership does not only reveal how you guide others. It also reveals how your design carries responsibility, shapes direction, and contributes to the flourishing of people and purpose when stewarded well.

Toward Faithful Leadership

Healthy leadership is not merely about influence or authority. It is about carrying responsibility with humility, wisdom, and faithfulness. Leadership can become a place where service deepens, trust grows, and others are strengthened through the way you lead.

“Whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant.” — Matthew 20:26

How the Core Reflections Often Respond to Pressure

Architect
Architects often respond to pressure by moving quickly toward action, clarity, or control of the situation. Their instinct is to create traction and direction when circumstances feel uncertain or constrained.

Artisan
Artisans often respond to pressure by interpreting what is happening beneath the surface and seeking a clearer understanding of the situation. Their instinct is to make sense of complexity before moving too quickly.

Shepherd
Shepherds often respond to pressure through heightened awareness of people, relational impact, and emotional strain. Their instinct is to protect connection, reduce harm, and care for those affected by the weight of the moment.

Steward
Stewards often respond to pressure by looking for order, dependability, and what must be maintained. Their instinct is to preserve stability, carry responsibility, and keep what matters from falling apart.

Your response to pressure may be strengthened or strained depending on specific capacity. When capacity is steady or abundant, pressure can sharpen focus and maturity. When capacity is limited or drained, urgency may amplify reactivity, fatigue, or imbalance.

Pressure does not only test your design. It also reveals where endurance, trust, and wise self leadership can grow when your design is stewarded well.

Toward Steadiness

Pressure is not only something to survive. It can also become a place where trust deepens, character strengthens, and steadiness is formed. Pressure can become an opportunity to respond with greater clarity, resilience, and dependence on God.

“Be joyful in hope, patient in affliction, faithful in prayer.” — Romans 12:12

Page 17

Your tendencies in Plan, Decide, and Do influence how you pace your efforts, how you interpret the demands placed upon you, and how you sustain action without losing clarity or purpose.

How the Core Reflections Often Approach Sustainability

Architect
Architects often sustain momentum by continuing to build, initiate, and pursue meaningful progress. Their instinct is to stay engaged through forward movement, vision, and the pursuit of meaningful outcomes.

Artisan
Artisans often sustain their design through clarity, reflection, and thoughtful interpretation of what truly matters. Their instinct is to maintain meaning, perspective, and understanding so their work remains purposeful.

Shepherd
Shepherds often sustain their design through relationships, encouragement, and shared care. Their instinct is to remain connected with people and community so that the journey is not carried alone.

Steward
Stewards often sustain their design through consistency, responsibility, and steady follow through. Their instinct is to maintain order, reliability, and faithful attention to what has been entrusted to them.

Sustainability grows as your reflections remain balanced and your capacities remain healthy. When your design is carried wisely, your influence becomes more stable, your relationships deepen, and your contribution continues to mature over time.

Sustaining your design well is not about constant activity. It is about pacing your strengths, recognizing limits, and stewarding the gifts God has given you so that your life continues to bear fruit.

Toward Faithful Endurance

True sustainability grows when your design remains rooted in trust, humility, and faithful stewardship of the life God has given you. Over time, steady faithfulness often produces deeper fruit than constant striving.

“Let us not become weary in doing good, for at the proper time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up.” — Galatians 6:9

Page 19

Design Alignment

Understanding your design helps clarify how you naturally plan, decide, and act. Design Alignment looks at how those tendencies interact with the people, responsibilities, and environments around you. When design and environment support one another, clarity increases, collaboration improves, and progress becomes more sustainable.

The MAPS Alignment Model

Mission
Purpose
Culture
Motivation
Approach
Assessment
Insight
Direction
Process
Proof
Organization
Reliability
Send
Energy
Momentum
Outcomes

Healthy alignment follows a clear progression. Mission clarifies what matters and where direction begins. Approach shapes how situations are understood and responded to. Process builds the systems and structure needed for consistency and reliability. Send moves insight into real-world action, creating momentum and measurable outcomes.

Your Design and Alignment

Plan → Mission + Approach
Your planning tendency ({{ plan_tendency | replace: "_", " " }}) often influences how you recognize direction, define what matters, and shape how you approach what is ahead.

Decide → Approach + Process
Your decision tendency ({{ decide_tendency | replace: "_", " " }}) often influences how situations are interpreted, options are clarified, and structure is established for what comes next.

Do → Send
Your action tendency ({{ do_tendency | replace: "_", " " }}) often influences how plans move into real-world execution, creating momentum and tangible results.

Your primary and secondary reflections ({{primary}} / {{secondary}}), and your integrative reflection ({{integrative_reflection}}), influence how your design moves through Mission, Approach, Process, and Send in real environments.

Alignment and Teams

Alignment is rarely created by one person alone. Teams often experience friction when one part of the MAPS model is overrepresented while another is missing. Some teams carry strong Mission but struggle to Send. Others build strong Process but lack clarity in their Approach. When individuals understand their design and teams learn how those designs work together, alignment becomes easier to recognize, strengthen, and sustain.

“Make every effort to keep the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace.” — Ephesians 4:3

Page 20

Continue the Work of Alignment

Insight is powerful. Alignment makes it actionable.

This report has introduced language for how your design tends to plan, decide, and act. It has also explored how these tendencies influence conflict, collaboration, leadership, pressure, and long term sustainability. Awareness is an important beginning, but alignment grows most deeply when insight is applied in real environments.

Many individuals and teams discover that the next step is not simply more information, but guided reflection and practical application. Coaching and alignment work help individuals lead with greater clarity while helping teams understand how different designs contribute to mission, approach, process, and send.
